content.stem: Prove that \[\frac{\tan^2\theta}{\sec\theta - 1} - \frac{\cot^2\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1} = \sec\theta - \operatorname{cosec}\theta + 2,\] where \(\theta\) is an acute angle.

hints: Each numerator can be rewritten using an identity involving the denominator's function: think of \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - \cot^2\theta = 1\).
After rewriting, look for a difference of two squares that cancels with the denominator.

steps.title: Simplify the first term
steps.explanation: Replace \(\tan^2\theta\) by \(\sec^2\theta - 1\), factorise as a difference of squares and cancel \((\sec\theta - 1)\), which is non-zero for an acute angle.

steps.title: Simplify the second term
steps.explanation: In the same way, replace \(\cot^2\theta\) by \(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - 1\), factorise and cancel \((\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1)\).

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: Subtract carefully: the minus sign in front of the bracket turns \(-1\) into \(+1\), which together with the other \(+1\) gives \(+2\).

commonMistakes: Writing \(\tan^2\theta = 1 - \sec^2\theta\) (wrong sign), which makes the cancellation fail.
Dropping the bracket in step 3 and writing \(\sec\theta + 1 - \operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1 = \sec\theta - \operatorname{cosec}\theta\).
Working on both sides at once and 'meeting in the middle' without showing that LHS reduces to RHS.

alternativeMethods.title: Convert to sines and cosines
alternativeMethods.description: \(\dfrac{\tan^2\theta}{\sec\theta - 1} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta/\cos^2\theta}{(1 - \cos\theta)/\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta(1 - \cos\theta)} = \dfrac{1 + \cos\theta}{\cos\theta} = \sec\theta + 1\), and similarly the second term equals \(\dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\sin\theta} = \operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1\). Then subtract as before.

criteria.description: Reduces the first term to sec θ + 1
criteria.expectedEvidence: Uses tan²θ = sec²θ − 1, factorises (secθ − 1)(secθ + 1) and cancels
acceptedAlternatives: Equivalent sin/cos working reaching (1 + cos θ)/cos θ

criteria.description: Reduces the second term to cosec θ − 1
criteria.expectedEvidence: Uses cot²θ = cosec²θ − 1, factorises and cancels
acceptedAlternatives: Equivalent sin/cos working reaching (1 − sin θ)/sin θ

criteria.description: Combines with correct signs and concludes LHS = RHS
criteria.partialCreditRules: Not awarded if the +2 appears without the sign working being shown, or if the student works on both sides without a valid chain.

questions.authorNotes: Restricting \(\theta\) to an acute angle keeps \(\sec\theta - 1 \neq 0\) so the cancellation is valid. Identity checked numerically at several angles.

content.stem: If \(\sec\theta + \tan\theta = \tfrac{5}{2}\), then the value of \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\) is

hints: Multiply \((\sec\theta + \tan\theta)\) by \((\sec\theta - \tan\theta)\). Which identity does the product remind you of?

steps.title: Use the identity
steps.explanation: The product of the sum and the difference is a difference of squares, which equals 1.

steps.title: Divide
steps.explanation: Divide 1 by the given value of the sum.

commonMistakes: (b) comes from using \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = -1\) (the identity with the sign reversed).
(d) comes from subtracting 1 from the sum instead of dividing 1 by it.
(a) assumes the difference equals the sum.

questions.authorNotes: Consistent with an acute angle: \(\sec\theta = \tfrac{29}{20}\), \(\tan\theta = \tfrac{21}{20}\), both positive and \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1\).
